description: Somos un equipo del Centro Universitario de Guadalajara, conformado por estudiantes de tecnologías biomédicas y finanzas, apasionados por la investigación de los efectos del espacio en la salud de los astronautas. Contamos con habilidades de tecnología e innovación, conocimientos avanzados sobre IA y soporte vital. En este reto buscamos ayudar a los astronautas con el monitorio de salud en el espacio y la guiarlos con instrucciones sencillas sobre como actuar en emergencias.
summary:
Space First AID monitors the health of each crew member during a long-duration mission, such as an Earth–Mars journey, and guides the crew. It tracks vital signs, the symptoms each astronaut reports, and the results of urine, blood, and saliva samples, and uses that information to detect, in time, health problems specific to spaceflight: space motion sickness, SANS, fluid redistribution, the bone–kidney axis, nephrolithiasis, immune dysregulation, chronic fatigue, behavioral decline, stress from isolation, and acute radiation syndrome.
When it identifies a risk, it launches an animated protocol that explains step by step how to respond to the emergency or accident. It also assesses attention, coordination, and vision through short games that use the camera, and records mood, stress, workload, and teamwork, because mental health is as important as physical health on an isolated mission.
details:
NASA acknowledges that on Mars missions, communication delays or outages will require crews to have an onboard clinical decision support system (Krihak et al., 2021). Space First AID is a concrete proposal to meet that need. Detecting a health problem early also protects mission safety, because it prevents a single sick person from putting the entire crew at risk.

The impact is not limited to space. The same idea could serve isolated, low-connectivity places such as Antarctic bases, oil platforms, ships, or rural communities. In addition, by organizing NASA information into a clear clinical methodology, the project has educational value for teaching space medicine.

Why is it creative and innovative?

Space First AID brings the physical and the mental together in one place. Most systems keep vital signs separate from behavioral health, but here they are cross-referenced, because stress and poor sleep also weaken the body's defenses. It also turns medical tests into games: the camera measures attention, coordination, and vision without extra equipment and in an engaging way, which helps crew members do them frequently. Its visual language, with a 3D model, color-coded circles, and animated protocols, makes health status readable at a glance. Finally, it is designed from the ground up to work without a signal: it starts from the real constraint of a trip to Mars instead of depending on the Internet.

The next step is to move from simulated data to real data, and for the app to learn from each crew member. As for device connectivity, the goal is to receive real-time data from medical equipment over the spacecraft's internal network, without manual entry, and to sync that information automatically with the ground medical team whenever a signal is available, while continuing to work when there is none.

New features and monitoring factors could also be added. The app could track the cabin environment, such as CO₂, radiation, noise, light, and temperature. It could keep a log of food and fluids, with alerts when calories, vitamin D, or water run low, and track exercise to protect bone and muscle.

The main limitation is that the available databases are small. There is little information on medical conditions, symptoms, and health risks in space. We also acknowledge that the software may contain errors or inaccuracies, due to the time and technical expertise constraints under which it was built. This is a prototype, not a medical device: its data has not been clinically validated, and it does not replace the judgment of the flight surgeon.
